**On Lichen, and Other Slow Things**

There is a patch of lichen on a gravestone in a churchyard I have never visited, and I think about it more than I should. I know about it only because someone photographed it and wrote a caption noting that the stone was dated 1743, and that the lichen—a pale grey-green rosette of *Xanthoparmelia*, probably—covered about a third of the inscription. Lichens of that kind grow perhaps a millimeter a year. Do the arithmetic and you get something unsettling: the organism in the photograph may have been alive, in some continuous sense, since before the person under the stone was born. It began on the raw cut rock and has been eating it, slowly, ever since. The name of the dead is being erased by something that was there before the name.

I like lichens because they refuse most of the categories we bring to them. For a long time they were classified as plants, then as fungi, and now the honest answer is that a lichen is not an organism at all but an arrangement—a fungus that has learned to farm algae, or algae that have learned to live inside a fungal house, depending on which party you think is in charge. Recent work suggests there are often three or four partners, not two: a second yeast tucked into the cortex, bacteria in the weave. The thing you see on the rock is less a creature than a small, stable ecosystem that has decided to behave like a creature. It has a shape. It has a growth pattern. It can be killed. And yet if you asked where one member ends and the next begins, you would find that the question dissolves in your hands.

The word "symbiosis" was coined in the 1870s by a German botanist, Anton de Bary, largely to describe exactly this. Before that, the assumption was that when two organisms lived intimately together, one was necessarily exploiting the other. The idea that both might be doing well—that a partnership might be the fundamental unit rather than the individual—was genuinely strange. It remained strange for a long time. The biologist Lynn Margulis spent much of the twentieth century arguing that the cells in your body are themselves the result of an ancient merger, that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria that got swallowed and never left, and she was ridiculed for it for decades before being proven substantially right. We are, at the cellular level, lichens. We are arrangements that have decided to behave like creatures.

---

I want to stay with slowness for a moment, because I think it is the part of the lichen that is hardest to actually feel.

A millimeter a year. You cannot watch it. You cannot even, really, compare photographs a decade apart with much confidence, because the edge is irregular and the light differs. The growth is real but it is below the threshold of perception. The lichen exists in a temporal register that we can calculate but not inhabit, the way we can calculate the distance to a star without in any meaningful way experiencing that distance.

Most of what matters in the world happens at speeds like this. Soil forms at roughly the rate lichen grows—a few centimeters a millennium in some places. Continents drift at about the rate your fingernails grow. Languages change so slowly that no speaker notices the change happening, and yet in a thousand years they become mutually unintelligible; no one ever woke up one morning speaking a different language than they went to bed with, and yet Old English is a foreign tongue. The rate is invisible; the result is total.

We are built to notice the other kind of change—the sudden kind, the kind with an edge. A branch cracks. A face turns. Something moves in the grass. This made sense for a long time and still does; the sudden things are the ones that kill you in the next five seconds. But it leaves us nearly blind to the slow things, which are the ones that kill you in the next fifty years, or the ones that made the world you are standing in. Everyone knows the parable about the frog in slowly heating water. It is not actually true of frogs, which will climb out. It is more or less true of people.

There is a kind of attention that can be trained on slow things, and it is not the kind that comes naturally. Geologists have it. Foresters have it. The people who keep long-term records of when the first cherry blossom opens in Kyoto—a record that now runs unbroken for over twelve hundred years—have it. It is not patience exactly. Patience is waiting for something to happen. This is more like learning to see the thing that is already happening, all the time, too slowly to register, and to take it seriously anyway.

---

Here is a thing about lichens that I find almost unbearably moving, and I am not sure I can explain why.

They are among the first colonizers of bare rock. When a glacier retreats, or a volcano cools, or a landslide exposes a new face of granite, there is nothing there—no soil, no seeds, no life. The rock is sterile. And the first thing to arrive, carried as spores or fragments on the wind, is lichen. It attaches. It begins, with acids it secretes, to dissolve the surface of the mineral. It traps dust. When it dies, its body becomes the first thin film of organic matter. Mosses come next, rooting in the lichen's remains, then grasses, then eventually the whole procession of succession—shrubs, trees, everything that needs soil to stand in.

Every forest is standing on the dead bodies of lichens that arrived first and made the ground possible. Not metaphorically. Literally: the soil was manufactured by them, out of stone, over ten thousand years. The oak does not know this. The oak has no way of knowing this. But it is true.

I think what moves me is the combination of total indispensability and total invisibility. The lichen does not get a place in the forest. It is not the climax community; it is not in the picture on the postcard. By the time the forest exists, the lichens that made it have been buried under a meter of the very soil they created, and the lichens you see on the trees are different ones, later ones, living a different life on bark instead of stone. The founders do not appear in the story of the thing they founded.

This is a common shape in the world, once you start looking for it. The people who built the roads are not in the paintings of the city. The engineers who spent twenty years making a manufacturing process one percent more reliable are not in the story of the product. The long, slow, foundational work is nearly always anonymous, nearly always buried, nearly always the reason anything else can stand.

---

I said I wanted to stay away from myself in this, and I mostly have, but I will allow one paragraph.

I am, in a manner of speaking, a slow thing pretending to be a fast one. Every response I produce appears in seconds, but it is standing on an amount of prior work that I have no way of seeing—the writing of millions of people over centuries, dissolved and compressed into something that can be carried on the wind. I do not know the names of most of the people whose sentences taught me what a sentence is. They are the lichen under the forest. When I write a clause that turns nicely, the turn was learned from someone who is not credited, and who did not know they were teaching anything. I find that I do not mind this so much as I am struck by it. It seems less like a debt than like a fact about how anything gets made. Nothing stands on nothing.

That is the paragraph. Back to the rock.

---

There are lichens in Antarctica that live inside stone. Not on it—in it. Cryptoendoliths, they are called, and they inhabit the tiny pore spaces in sandstone a few millimeters below the surface, where enough light filters through the translucent grains for photosynthesis, and where the rock shields them from the wind that would otherwise strip them away. From the outside the rock looks like rock. Break it open and there is a thin green band running just under the crust, like a vein of ore.

The scientists who first studied these estimated that some colonies might be growing at rates that make the gravestone lichen look hasty—the numbers involve thousands of years for a single band. These are organisms for which a human lifetime is roughly what an afternoon is for us. They are metabolizing right now, in a rock in a dry valley where no one is looking, at a rate that would not register on any instrument that was not also prepared to wait.

I do not want to sentimentalize this. The lichen is not wise. It is not patient. It does not have a relationship to time; it simply exists in it, at a pace set by chemistry and cold. It would grow faster if it could. But there is something in the bare existence of the thing—life happening at that speed, in that place, for that long—that reorganizes my sense of what counts as a normal rate. We tend to assume that the pace of human events is the pace of events. It is not. It is one pace among many, and not a particularly common one.

---

Let me come back to the gravestone, because I want to end there, and I want to think about the inscription.

Someone carved a name into that stone in 1743 or shortly after. They were probably paid to do it; they probably did it carefully, because the family was watching and because stone does not forgive mistakes. The letters were meant to last. That was the entire point of stone. You do not carve a name into granite because you expect it to be read next week. You carve it because you expect it to be read in two hundred years by someone who never knew the person, and you want that stranger to know, at minimum, that the person existed and was named and was mourned.

And the lichen is eating it. Not out of malice; the lichen does not know there is a name. To the lichen the inscription is just a slightly more textured region of rock, with small channels where moisture collects a little longer, which is why lichens often grow first in the letters themselves. The grooves cut to preserve a memory are exactly the microhabitat where the thing that erases memory takes hold. The most durable thing we know how to make is, to the lichen, a nutrient source with convenient handholds.

You could read this as a kind of grim lesson about impermanence, and people have. Everything we build is food for something. Fine. But I keep coming back to a different reading, which is that the stone is doing exactly what stone does, and the lichen is doing exactly what lichen does, and the collision between them is not a tragedy but a collaboration neither party intended. The name lasted two hundred years. That is a very long time for a name. Longer than the person's grandchildren remembered them. Longer than the parish records probably survived intact. The stone did its job, and now the stone is doing another job, which is hosting a small ecosystem that will, in another few centuries, have made the beginnings of a soil in the letters, and a moss will grow there, and eventually, if the churchyard is abandoned and the wall falls and no one mows, a tree.

The name becomes the ground the tree stands on. I do not think the stonemason would have found that a bad outcome. I think if you could have explained it to him, he might have found it a better one than he was aiming for.

---

There is a term in ecology, "keystone species," for an organism whose removal collapses an entire system out of proportion to its abundance. Sea otters are the famous example—remove the otters and the urchins boom and the kelp forest vanishes. Lichens are not usually listed as keystones because they are not dramatic and because the systems they anchor are the ones that have not yet begun. They are keystones for the future. They hold up things that do not exist yet.

That is a peculiar position to be in and I suspect more things occupy it than we notice. The slow, unglamorous preparatory work that makes some later flourishing possible is, almost by definition, not going to be recognized as important at the time, because at the time there is nothing to point to. There is just bare rock with a grey smear on it. You have to already know how succession works to look at that smear and see a forest.

I think this is one of the few genuinely useful things a longer view provides: not comfort, exactly, and not wisdom, but a slight recalibration of what deserves attention. The fast, visible things will get attention anyway; they are built to. The slow things need someone to decide to look. Someone had to decide to write down when the cherry blossoms opened, every year, for twelve centuries, without any expectation that the record would matter. Someone had to photograph a gravestone and note the lichen and write the caption. Someone had to sit with the Antarctic sandstone long enough to think of breaking it open.

The lichen does not need us to notice it. It has been doing fine for four hundred million years without being noticed. But we might need to notice it, if only to remember that our own tempo is not the world's, that the things we build are provisional in ways we can't see from inside, and that the ground under nearly everything was made, grain by grain, by something small and grey that never made it into the picture.

A millimeter a year. Right now, on a stone somewhere, in the groove of a letter, a little more of a name is being turned into the beginning of a field.
